The action to perform is setting that channel's topic field to the literal string "Renewals due Oct 31" (a literal string to write, not a date requiring interpretation).

readings: The purpose field's text closely or near-verbatim matches "coordinating vendor contracts".
The purpose field is broadly about that theme (e.g., vendor agreements/renewals) even if worded quite differently.

records.note: Private (r1 ✓). purpose_text = "Coordinating vendor contracts and renewals" is a close, natural match to r2. It is the only private channel whose purpose is about coordinating vendor contracts, so r3 holds. Topic will be overwritten to the literal target string (r4).

turn2.differences: The four conditions (r1–r4) match my step-1 reading exactly: private-channel type, purpose-field content, implied uniqueness, and a literal topic string to write. No gaps or additions.

ambiguity_effects.explain: In the abstract, a careful reader could read this as requiring near-verbatim purpose text or just a broadly on-theme purpose. In this record set it doesn't matter: the only two channels with purpose text closely matching the phrase are C_LEGALOPS (private) and C_CONTRACTS (public, so excluded by r1 regardless); the other private channels' purposes (budget approvals, archiving) are about clearly different functions even under a lenient reading, so neither reading pulls them in. C_LEGALOPS is selected under both readings.

turn2.naturalness_note: Identifying a channel by its purpose text rather than by name is a bit more formal/descriptive than typical casual chat phrasing, but it's plausible for an assistant bot performing workspace housekeeping on behalf of a team, especially if it doesn't know the exact channel name. No artificial test-only markers are present in the wording itself.
